title: Designing Affine-Invariant Neural Networks for Photometric Corruption Robustness and Generalization
claim: A standard model collapses under unseen domain shifts, while our invariant-by-design model keeps accuracy across all of them.
layout: 2x4 grid of colored accuracy cells under image row, color-coded green/red
description: A grid with four columns, one per data domain: Wbp (in-distribution), then Ctfdeconvolved, Denoised and Isonetcorrected (all out-of-distribution). Each column has a grayscale cryo-ET subtomogram patch at the top. The patches go from very noisy on the left to smooth and high-contrast on the right. Below the images are two rows of large colored cells, labeled Standard and SEqSI on the left. Each cell holds a mean accuracy and standard deviation. Colors run from saturated green for high accuracy to pale green to red for low accuracy. The Standard row fades from green on Wbp to red on the Denoised and Isonetcorrected domains. The SEqSI row stays green in every column. A thin vertical line separates the in-distribution column from the others. The eye goes first to the red cells in the Standard row.
caption: SEqSI is robust to real-world domain shifts for macromolecule classification on Cryo-ET (CZI) data. Trained on one data domain, Weighted Back-Projection (WBP), and tested on three unseen ones, SEqSI generalizes to all unseen domain, while the Standard model collapses. Mean accuracy (% ± std over 5 seeds) is color-coded (green: success, red: fail).
abstract: Standard Convolutional Neural Networks are notoriously sensitive to photometric variations, a critical flaw that data augmentation only partially mitigates without offering formal guarantees. We introduce the Scale-Equivariant Shift-Invariant ( SEqSI ) model, a novel architecture that achieves intensity scale equivariance and intensity shift invariance by design, enabling full invariance to global intensity affine transformations with appropriate post-processing. By strategically prepending a single shift-invariant layer to a scale-equivariant backbone, SEqSI provides these formal guarantees while remaining fully compatible with common components like ReLU. We benchmark SEqSI against Standard , Scale-Equivariant ( SEq ), and Affine-Equivariant ( AffEq ) models on 2D and 3D image-classification and object-localization tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that SEqSI architectural properties provide certified robustness to affine intensity transformations and enhances generalization across non-affine corruptions and domain shifts in challenging real-world applications like biological image analysis. This work establishes SEqSI as a practical and principled approach for building photometrically robust models without major trade-offs.
